revisions.body:
Can your champion explain your ROI in one sentence?

Someone asked a CS forum which habit does the most for renewals. Onboarding, adoption reviews, health scoring or proactive support.

I read all 25 replies. Every option got votes.

My answer is none of them, at least not on their own.

Customers don't renew because they used the product. They renew when their champion can tell the CFO, in dollars, what it paid back.

Each habit only works when it serves that.

1/ Onboarding is where you learn what value means to this customer. Skip that and you've just configured software.

2/ Adoption reviews should show the value delivered. Logins don't count as value.

3/ Health scores should tell you whether the customer is getting that value. Plenty of busy accounts still churn.

4/ Proactive support keeps people from getting frustrated. It doesn't give anyone a reason to stay.

You need all four pointed at the same number. A customer can log in daily and still leave, and a customer who never complains can still leave.

If you're explaining the ROI for the first time 90 days before renewal, you're already late.

So which habit has done the most for your renewals?
revisions.claim_safe_proposal:
A customer can use the product every day and still struggle to explain why they're paying for it.

I'd ask the champion to show one result the business would lose if it stopped.

Then make that result easy to pass on. What changed, what evidence supports it, and what part the product played.

Keep the limits in the explanation too. Don't claim the whole result if the customer's team did most of the work.

That gives the champion something useful for the internal conversation. A login chart alone leaves them to build the argument.

What would you want in that handover before renewal?

revisions.body:
Nobody trains CSMs for the day a customer leaves.

We get trained on onboarding, renewals, expansion and QBRs. Then a customer says "we've decided to move on," and most of us have no playbook at all.

What usually follows is a slow fade. Replies take longer and the calls get shorter. Nobody is rude, but the customer can feel the team stepping back.

That's the last thing they remember about you.

I think that's a waste. The contract ended, but the people didn't go anywhere. Your champion will change jobs and pick vendors again. Their team still has to migrate off your platform. And some customers come back within a year, once the new tool turns out to be harder than the demo.

So the last 30 days deserve real effort.

→ Help with the data export, the admin handover and the licence cleanup. A messy exit is the story they'll tell their peers.

→ Keep the same response times, the same tone and the same person on the calls. The commercial side is finished, and the relationship doesn't have to be.

→ Send a short, honest wrap-up. What worked, what didn't, and what to watch for with the next vendor. One page is plenty.

→ Leave the door open once. One line saying you're around if they need anything, and no win-back pitch.

That wrap-up note matters more than it looks. If they ever need to argue internally for coming back, it's the document someone will forward.

You lose the account either way. How you leave decides whether they ever pick up the phone again.
revisions.claim_safe_proposal:
A customer leaving still needs a clear last day.

I'd agree the exit work while there's time to do it: who handles the export, who takes over admin access and which support route remains available.

Check the contract and the customer's security process before promising help. If something needs a separate agreement, say so.

Then leave a short record of what's finished, what's still open and who owns it.

The customer shouldn't have to chase a departing account team for that answer.

What belongs in your final handover?
